title: What if I encounter a Sasquatch while Christmas tree hunting?
excerpt: Since the Rotary Club lost its Christmas tree supplier, obtaining a fresh tree has become a bit of a quandary in Prince Rupert. With limited supply, prices look to be […]
content:
Published 5:30 am Thursday, November 26, 2026

By Thom Barker/Prince Rupert

Since the Rotary Club lost its Christmas tree supplier, obtaining a fresh tree has become a bit of a quandary in Prince Rupert. With limited supply, prices look to be about tripled, which puts these single-use items up into the range of quality synthetics that can last decades.

At that point, the question becomes, do we just go and get one of those high end artificial trees and be done with it?

There really isn’t anything quite like the real thing, though, is there?

The good news is, anyone can go and cut their own tree on Crown land for personal use. In researching this, I came across a quirky thing about provincial regulations.

You need a “free use permit” to go cut down a tree. However, there is no application process. You can simply go to the Government of B.C. website, download the permit and print it.

Basically, this is government red tape at its finest. A bureaucratic hurdle with no registration or tracking. Fundamentally, it’s the honour system, although, if you don’t have the piece of paper, there could be unspecified consequences.

I am not in any way complaining about this. I just find it amusing.

We are very much looking forward to going out tree hunting. Somehow, the process of actually taking a saw and going out on a family outing to select a tree, cut it down and haul it home is really enhancing our Christmas spirit.

It got me thinking about what other oddities might be lurking in the laws and regulations of our fine province. Good thing I went looking, just in case we run into a Sasquatch while we’re out tree hunting.

Legend has it that, at one time, B.C. had a statute on the books specifically outlawing shooting the legendary furry humanoids also known as Bigfoot.

There has never been any evidence produced that such a law existed, at least not in B.C.

However, Skamania County, in neighbouring Washington State, did pass an ordinance in 1969 (updated in 1984 and still on the books) making it illegal to kill a Bigfoot punishable by a $1,000 fine and/or one year in jail.

Now, I wouldn’t want to kill a Sasquatch if I encountered it, except perhaps in self-defence (not to mention the fact it is a mythical creature that doesn’t exist).

Despite, the mythological nature of the Sasquatch, and the lack of legislation on the B.C. books dealing with the killing thereof, speculation abounds about the consequences of such an act.

In 2025, the publication Vancouver is Awesome, did a deep dive into the question. To do so, they consulted Kyla Lee, a Vancouver criminal lawyer.

Her conclusions were complicated.

If you were hunting Sasquatch, she says you’d have to have a hunting licence and the proper tags, although Sasquatch tags don’t exist. And, of course, you’d have to have the requisite possession and acquisition licence to do it with a firearm.

You’d also have to be in an area where hunting is legal.

Self-defence would be acceptable, as would killing it to protect your farm or crops, but in that case, you’d have to take all reasonable steps to protect them in other ways first, then obtain a permit.

Lee also raised the point of whether or not Sasquatches are human, in which case, killing one could result in murder or manslaughter charges.

“In summary, my legal advice to anybody considering hunting or killing a Sasquatch would be not to do so, because of the unanswered question of its humanity,” she told Vancouver is Awesome.

Advice taken. I will stick to hunting a Christmas tree.
